What is the International Fixed Calendar?
The International Fixed Calendar (IFC) reshapes the year into 13 months of exactly 28 days each — four whole weeks, every month, every year, forever.
The extra, 13th month is called Sol, and it sits between June and July.
Because every month is exactly 4 weeks, every month starts on a nominal Sunday and ends on a nominal Saturday — and the 13th of every month nominally falls on a Friday.
The two days outside the week
13 months of 28 days add up to 364 days — one short of a full year, two short in a leap year. Those extra days do not belong to any week or month; the IFC sets them apart as Year Day and Leap Day.
Year Day happens every year. It comes after December 28 and before next January 1 — it belongs to no week and has no IFC weekday of its own. %1$s is Gregorian %2$s.
Leap Day happens only in leap years. It comes after June 28 and before Sol 1 — also outside the week. %1$s is Gregorian %2$s.
Why the weekdays in this app differ

The IFC gets its perpetual weekdays by taking Year Day and Leap Day out of the week entirely. The real world does not do this: the seven-day cycle runs on, unbroken, through December 31 and June 17 every year.
For example: %1$s is IFC %2$s. Its IFC weekday is %3$s, but because Year Day (and, in leap years, Leap Day) are taken out of the count first, its real weekday is %4$s.

This is why the app always shows both weekdays: the IFC one for the calendar\'s own sense of the week, and the real one for anything tied to actual life — today\'s highlight, your events, and your reminders.
How the dates are calculated

The IFC\'s day-of-year number is always identical to the Gregorian one. The calendar\'s own numeric date form always carries an \"IFC\" marker, like %1$s, so it can never be mistaken for an ordinary Gregorian date written the same way.
Sol 1 is always Gregorian June 18, whether the year is a leap year or not: %1$s is Gregorian %2$s, and %3$s is Gregorian %4$s.
Year Day is always Gregorian December 31: %1$s is Gregorian %2$s.

In a leap year, Leap Day is inserted after June 28, which pushes every IFC date from March through June one day later than in a common year. For example, Gregorian March 1 is %1$s in a common year like %2$d, but %3$s in a leap year like %4$d.
And because every month is exactly 4 weeks, the 13th of every month is always a nominal Friday: %1$s\'s IFC weekday is %2$s.
A brief history

Moses B. Cotsworth (1859–1943), a British railway statistician, devised the plan so that monthly figures could be compared fairly, and presented it in 1902; his book explaining it, \"The Rational Almanac,\" is dated 1902 or 1905 depending on the source.

The League of Nations took up calendar reform in the 1920s. According to Wikipedia, its committee judged the 13-month plan the best of 130 proposals and held an international conference on it in October 1931 — but it was never adopted, largely because days outside the week broke the continuous seven-day week observed by several religions.

George Eastman became the plan\'s main backer in the mid-1920s and put it to work at Eastman Kodak starting in 1928; Kodak\'s 13-period calendar stayed in internal use for decades — until around 1989, by most accounts.
No country has ever adopted the International Fixed Calendar.
Frequently asked questions
Is the IFC based on the phases of the moon?
No. Despite having 13 months, the IFC is a solar calendar: its year is exactly as long as the Gregorian year, and its months are fixed at 28 days regardless of the moon\'s roughly 29.5-day cycle.
Does the IFC year start in spring?
No. IFC January 1 is Gregorian January 1, the same as every other year — the IFC relabels the days inside the existing Gregorian year rather than starting the year somewhere else.
Are Sol and Leap Day the same thing?

No, they\'re different kinds of thing. Sol is a full, 28-day month between June and July, present every year. Leap Day is a single day with no week and no month, present only in leap years, coming after June 28.
Is this the only 13-month calendar?

No. Other 13-month proposals exist — among them the Positivist calendar, the World Calendar (which actually has 12 months) and the Pax calendar — and each places its extra days differently, or keeps the seven-day week intact instead. If a 13-month calendar has a month called Sol between June and July, a Year Day on Gregorian December 31 and a Leap Day on Gregorian June 17, it is this one, the IFC; otherwise, it\'s a different calendar.
What does the converter\'s note about \"proleptic\" dates mean?

For any date before a country actually adopted the Gregorian calendar, the app still uses today\'s calendar rules extended backward in time — historians call this \"proleptic.\" It lets the converter answer for any year from 1 to 9999, but a date from, say, the 1600s is a hypothetical translation, not a date anyone alive then would have recognized.

Privacy

In short

Your calendar stays on your phone. Yearal has no account, no ads, no analytics and no crash-reporting service — and because it has no permission to use the internet at all, nothing it stores could leave your device even if it wanted to.
What is stored, and where
Your settings, your events and your reminders are the only things this app keeps, and they live only in the app\'s own private storage on your device — never on a server, because there is no server.
Permissions, and what they\'re for

Restart the day at midnight: the app asks Android for permission to run right after your device restarts (\"receive boot completed\"), only so it can re-arm the alarm that keeps the widget and the date rollover correct — a restart otherwise cancels it.
Keep the widget\'s date right: a system mechanism the widget\'s background updates rely on (\"wake lock\") briefly keeps the device awake long enough to redraw the widget, so it never goes stale.
That\'s the complete list. Yearal does not ask for your contacts, your location, your photos or files, your device calendars, or the internet.
Backups

If you have Android device backup turned on with a screen lock set, your settings and events may be included in an encrypted backup to your Google account — encrypted with your own screen lock, so Google cannot read it either. You can turn this off at any time in your device\'s system settings; the app has no separate control over it.
